unit.title: Operate in an autonomous team environment

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: On a self-managed electrical crew, who plans the day-to-day order of work?
options: The client, who phones the crew each morning
The power company's engineer on the next job
The supplier who delivers the cable and fittings
The crew, within targets set by management

questions.stem: Four electricians in a team will all work on the same distribution board. How should its isolator be locked off?
options: One lock from the team leader covers the whole team
Each worker fits their own lock to a multi-lock hasp
The isolator handle is taped firmly in the off position
A sign saying 'Men at work' is hung on the board

questions.stem: In a group lock-off, when may the isolator be switched back on?
options: When the team leader thinks the work is nearly done
When the first worker has finished and removed a lock
When every worker has removed their own lock
When the client asks to have the supply back

questions.stem: A worker's padlock is still on the isolator, but he has gone home with the key. What should happen?
options: The authorised lock-removal procedure, starting by contacting him
Cut the lock off, as he has probably finished his part
Open it with a spare key from the store and say nothing
Leave the lock on and switch on at the next board upstream

questions.stem: The team's skills matrix shows that only one member can program the new lighting controller. What should the team plan?
options: Train a second member while the job goes on
Turn down any job that has a lighting controller
Let anyone try it and fix the mistakes afterwards
Ask the client to program the controller themselves

questions.stem: Which target for a classroom rewiring job is written best?
options: Work as hard as possible and finish the block soon
Do neater wiring than every other team in the Centre
Wire and test 24 sockets in Block B by Friday 4 p.m.
Get as many sockets done as we can before the weekend

questions.stem: The team must terminate armoured cables, which only Shauna has done before. Which plan builds the team's skills without risking the job?
options: Let Shauna do every termination on every job from now on
Pair Shauna with a newer member, and she checks each one
Give it to the newest member to learn by trial and error
Leave it until the instructor has time to do it for the team

questions.stem: Which decision should a self-managed electrical team refer to the designer or manager, rather than make itself?
options: The order in which the rooms will be wired
Who collects the materials from the store
When the team takes its morning break
Changing a cable size shown on the drawing

questions.stem: Halfway through a job, a member's tester shows voltage on a circuit the team believed was dead. What should happen?
options: Carry on carefully, using insulated tools and gloves
Assume the tester is faulty, swap it, and carry on
Stop, warn the team, and find the source before going on
Switch off the next breaker along and carry on with the work

questions.stem: When is it right for one person to decide for the team at once, without discussion?
options: When the team cannot agree where to have lunch
In an emergency, such as a fire or an electric shock
When one member disagrees with the rest of the team
Whenever a task is dull and nobody wants to discuss it

questions.stem: A team member has received a shock and is still in contact with the live conductor. What should the others do first?
options: Grab him by the arm and pull him clear at once
Throw water over him to cool the burn
Run to find the instructor and wait for them
Switch off the supply, without touching him

questions.stem: At the end of the day, a pair has left a circuit half-terminated. How should they hand it over to the pair taking over tomorrow?
options: Label it 'not complete' and brief the next pair
Say nothing, since the next pair will spot it themselves
Leave it, and mention it only if anyone asks
Send a short voice note to one of the pair

questions.stem: A team has started to agree its ways of working, and members now accept each other's roles. Which stage of team development is this usually called?
options: Forming
Norming
Storming
Adjourning

questions.stem: Two members start arguing in front of a client about which of them made a wiring mistake. What should a Level 3 member do?
options: Join in and back whichever one seems to be right
Tell the client which of the two is to blame
Stop it there, and deal with it privately later
Ignore it and carry on with your own work

questions.stem: Several new circuits fail their insulation resistance test. What is the best first step for the team?
options: Collect the facts: which circuits, what readings, which routes
Pull out and replace every cable on the floor straight away
Use a lower test voltage until the readings come out higher
Blame the cable supplier and send the drums back today

questions.stem: Which tool helps a team sort the possible causes of a problem into groups, such as people, methods, materials and equipment?
options: A Gantt chart of the job
A skills matrix for the team
A daily site diary
A cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram

questions.stem: In a month, inspection finds: loose terminals 18, missing labels 9, wrong conductor identification 3, damaged sheaths 2. Which should the team tackle first?
options: Damaged sheaths, because they happen least often
Wrong identification, because it is easiest to spot
Loose terminals: the most common, and a fire risk
All four at once, giving each the same effort

questions.stem: A team uses a sheet on which a second member initials each circuit after checking it. What is the main benefit?
options: Faults are caught early, and the check is recorded
The first member no longer needs to check their own work
The circuits will not need testing afterwards
The manager can see which member is fastest

questions.stem: Which item matters most on an electrical team's start-of-day meeting agenda?
options: Last night's football results and the latest league table
Today's tasks, today's hazards and who holds each lock
Overtime pay claims from last month's big job
Who is buying lunch and where it is coming from

questions.stem: A member says a co-worker has been using a damaged extension lead all week. What should the team do?
options: Wrap the damage in tape and keep using the lead
Leave it until the weekly tool inspection is done
Tell the co-worker to be more careful with it
Tag it 'Do not use', remove it and report it

questions.stem: A female trainee on the team is always given the paperwork and never the wiring. What should the team do?
options: Keep it that way, since she does the paperwork well
Let her stay on office jobs for the rest of the course
Ask the client which members should do the wiring
Share tasks fairly, using the skills matrix

questions.stem: Two teams both need the Centre's only insulation resistance tester on Thursday. What is the best way to settle it?
options: Whichever team gets to the store first keeps it all day
Agree times with the other team and book them in the log
Borrow a tester from a friend's company without asking anyone
Skip the insulation test this week and do it next week

questions.stem: The client has added extra circuits, and the team will need two more days than planned. What should it do?
options: Work late every night without telling the manager
Leave the client's extra circuits out of the job
Tell the manager now, with the reason and a new date
Rush the work and leave all of the testing until the end

questions.stem: The team's job sheets show that terminating a distribution board always takes twice as long as planned. What should it do?
options: Find out why, and plan future boards realistically
Keep the same plan and tell everyone to go faster
Stop writing down the times so it no longer shows
Pass all board work over to another team in future

questions.stem: Why should feedback on a member's work be given soon after the job, rather than weeks later?
options: So that the manager never hears about it
So that it can be forgotten more quickly
So the member remembers the work and can act on it
So that it can be given in front of the client and the team

questions.stem: A new member from another trade joins the team. Before he works on any circuit, what must he know?
options: The team's isolation and lock-off procedure
Which radio station the team likes to play
Where each member parks in the morning
The manager's home address and phone number

questions.stem: Who in a self-managed team answers for the accuracy of a test result that a member records?
options: Only the manager, who signs the job off
The client, who receives the certificate
The inspector, who will check it later anyway
The member who tested, and the one who checked

questions.stem: At the end of a team meeting, which record is most useful?
options: A list of who spoke the most and the least
Each action agreed, who will do it and by when
The time the meeting began and when it ended
The names of anyone who arrived late

questions.stem: A member suggests making up the earth fly-leads for all the socket boxes on the bench before going on site. How should the team treat the idea?
options: Try it on one floor, compare results, then decide
Reject it, because the old way has always worked well enough
Use it on every floor at once without checking
Leave it for the manager to decide next month

questions.stem: Which measure best shows whether a team's wiring is right first time?
options: The hours of overtime worked each week
The number of cable drums used each month
The share of circuits passing tests first time
The number of tools carried in the van

questions.stem: Why does a team keep a 'lessons learned' log from each job?
options: So it can find out whom to blame for each mistake
So good ideas and mistakes are used on the next job
So the filing cabinet has something in it
Because every client asks to see one at the handover meeting

questions.stem: Near the end of a long day, a tired member wants to finish terminating a board. Why might the team leave it until the morning?
options: Hand tools work better in the cooler morning air
The client may be asleep and need quiet
Boards may not be wired after 5 p.m. by law
Tired people make more mistakes in careful work

questions.stem: The client asks a team member to add a socket that is not on the drawing. What should the member do?
options: Add it, because the client is paying for the job
Refuse, and tell the client to stop interfering
Ignore the request and hope it is forgotten
Explain it must be agreed with the team leader

questions.stem: The plumbers on site plan to cut an opening where your team's conduit runs. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Let them cut it and re-run the conduit later
Stand in the way until they give up
Meet them, check the drawings and agree a route
Move your conduit quietly overnight

questions.stem: Who in a self-managed team should check each day that the first-aid kit and fire extinguisher are in place?
options: The member who has that duty on the rota
Nobody, because the Centre's staff check them every week
The client, whose building it is
Always the newest member of the team

questions.stem: Why does a self-managed team rotate the role of 'safety lead' among its members?
options: To slow the job down so that it is all done more carefully
So everyone learns the duty and nobody gets careless
Because the Centre has no safety rules of its own
So that one person can do less work than the rest

questions.stem: A member thinks the day's plan is unsafe but is afraid to say so. What should the team do so this does not happen?
options: Warn members that disagreeing will be noted
Make clear anyone can raise a concern and be heard
Let only the team leader speak at meetings
Hold team meetings less often than before

questions.stem: A member's terminations have failed inspection three times this week. What is the best first step for the team?
options: Talk with him privately and agree support
Ask the manager to remove him from the team
Keep the results away from the manager
Redo his work quietly without telling him

questions.stem: While the team works in an occupied home in Portmore, what is expected of it?
options: Music played loudly so the team keeps up a good working pace
Free use of the client's tools, chairs and fridge
Respect for the home, a clean safe area and updates
Cables left across the floor ready for tomorrow

questions.stem: The team's daily output chart shows a drop every Monday. What should the team do?
options: Leave Mondays out of the chart from now on
Agree to work only four days each week
Put the Monday drop down to the weather
Look at what is different on Mondays

questions.stem: Why should a team review its skills matrix before taking on a new type of job, such as a solar PV installation?
options: To find gaps and plan training before the job
To decide which members should be let go
To complete a form that nobody reads
To find a reason to raise the price

questions.stem: During a rewiring job in an old building, the team finds that the main earthing conductor is missing. What should it do?
options: Carry on, since earthing is not part of the job as priced
Fit a new one quietly and tell nobody
Stop related work, record it and report it at once
Note it in the diary to look at next year

questions.stem: Which way of handling a disagreement between two members usually works best?
options: Wait and hope the problem goes away
Hear both views, look at the facts, agree a way forward
Let the louder member have the final say
Ask the manager to dismiss one of them

questions.stem: Why should a self-managed team keep a daily site diary?
options: To keep the jokes told on site
To take the place of the drawings
To save time on the job
To record work, problems and instructions

questions.stem: Why must a self-managed team's targets fit the company's wider plans?
options: So the team's work helps the whole business
So the team can ignore the plans of the other teams
So the team no longer needs a manager
So the targets never have to change

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: Name the fitting, with several holes, that is clipped onto an isolator so each worker can add a personal padlock.
Which stage of team development is reached when members work well together with little supervision?
What do we call the chart that shows which team members have which skills?
What is the name of the label fixed with a lock-off to show who isolated a circuit and why?
A team wired 108 points in 4 days. What was its average number of points per day?
What one word describes a team that manages itself with little direct supervision?
What do we call a short safety talk given to the team on site, often before work starts, about one hazard?
What word is used for a change to the agreed work, such as extra circuits asked for by the client, that must be agreed and priced?
What chart shows the tasks of a job as horizontal bars along a timeline?
In a RACI chart of team roles, what word does the letter R stand for?
What one word describes feedback that helps a person improve, rather than only criticising?
What is the name of the written permission, used on some sites, that must be issued before high-risk electrical work starts?
What word names the agreed date and time by which a task must be finished?
What is the usual name for the short meeting held at the end of a job to look at what went well and what to improve?
What word names a way of settling a disagreement in which each side gives up something to reach agreement?

essays.stem: Four members of your team will work at the same time on circuits fed from one distribution board. Describe how the team isolates the board safely, and explain why each worker uses their own lock.
essays.modelAnswer: First the team agrees which board and circuits are to be worked on and tells anyone affected. One member switches off the main isolator for the board. A multi-lock hasp is fitted to the isolator, and each of the four workers fits their own padlock and their own danger tag with their name, the date and the reason. Each keeps their own key. Then the board is proved dead: the voltage tester is checked on a proving unit, every conductor is tested, including line to neutral, line to earth and neutral to earth, and the tester is checked again on the proving unit. Only then does work start. Each worker uses their own lock because nobody else can then switch on while that worker is still exposed. When a worker finishes, they remove only their own lock. The isolator can be switched on only after every lock has been removed and the team has checked that everyone is clear and the work is safe to energise.
markingPoints: Isolator switched off and a multi-lock hasp fitted
Each worker fits their own lock and tag and keeps their own key
Proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after
Explains why: nobody can switch on while any worker is still exposed
Supply restored only after every lock is removed and everyone is clear

essays.stem: Your team of five has two weeks to rewire eight classrooms at a school in Spanish Town. Explain how the team would plan and organise the work itself.
essays.modelAnswer: The team first reads the drawings and specification and walks the site to see access, hazards and when classrooms are free. It breaks the job into tasks: removing old wiring, installing conduit or trunking, drawing in cables, fitting accessories, terminating the boards, testing and handover. It sets clear targets, for example one classroom wired and tested each day, leaving time for testing and snags. Tasks are shared by the skills matrix, pairing less experienced members with skilled ones, and a safety lead is named on a rota. Materials are worked out and ordered early so nothing holds the job up. Isolation rules are agreed with the school, so pupils are never near open work. The plan is shown on a Gantt chart or a progress board, checked at a short meeting each morning. Problems are reported to the manager early, and any changes the school asks for are agreed in writing.
markingPoints: Studies drawings, specification and site before planning
Breaks the job into tasks with clear, measurable targets
Shares tasks by skill and pairs members for training; names a safety lead
Plans materials, isolation and safety around the school
Tracks progress daily and reports problems or changes

essays.stem: A month after handover, a client reports that the RCD in the new installation trips several times a week. Explain how your team would use a problem-solving method to find and fix the cause.
essays.modelAnswer: The team would first define the problem clearly: which RCD, how often it trips, at what times and what was in use. It would collect facts by talking to the client and checking the test records from the handover. Then it lists the possible causes, for example a faulty appliance, moisture in an outdoor socket or light, too much normal leakage from many electronic loads on one RCD, a neutral-to-earth fault, or a faulty RCD. With the installation safely isolated, the team carries out dead tests such as insulation resistance on each circuit to narrow down the cause. An authorised person tests the RCD itself. When the cause is found, for example water in an outdoor box, the team fixes it and retests. It then checks with the client over the next weeks that the tripping has stopped. Finally, it records the cause and changes its normal practice, such as using better-sealed outdoor boxes on future jobs.
markingPoints: Defines the problem and collects facts
Lists likely causes (appliance, moisture, leakage, neutral-earth fault, faulty RCD)
Tests safely: isolated, dead tests, RCD test by an authorised person
Fixes the cause and checks the result over time
Records the cause and changes future practice

essays.stem: A team member says that proving dead on every circuit 'wastes time' and wants the team to skip it on small jobs. Others disagree, and tempers are rising. Explain how a Level 3 member should handle this.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first make it clear that safe isolation is not open to vote: every circuit is switched off, locked off and tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked before and after, on every job, because a circuit can be live from a wrong label, a borrowed neutral or a second supply. Until this is settled, nobody works on that circuit. Then I would calm the discussion and move it away from the client or the work area. I would let the member explain why he feels it wastes time, and listen properly, because he may have a real point about how the work is organised. I would explain the reasons with facts, for example real cases of electricians hurt on circuits they thought were dead. We might find ways to make the checks quicker, such as having testers and proving units ready at each job. If he still refuses to follow the procedure, I report it to the manager, because it puts the team at risk.
markingPoints: States that safe isolation is not negotiable and gives its steps
Stops work on the circuit until it is settled
Calms the conflict and listens respectfully to the member's view
Explains the reasons with facts and looks for practical ways to help
Reports to the manager if the unsafe practice continues

essays.stem: Explain how a self-managed electrical team should keep a client informed during a job, and how it should handle the client's requests for changes.
essays.modelAnswer: The team agrees at the start who will speak for it to the client, so the client gets one clear message. That person gives regular updates, for example at the end of each day or week, on what is done, what is next, and any problems such as delays in materials. The client is warned in good time before the power is switched off in occupied buildings. When the client asks for a change, such as an extra socket or a different light fitting, the team member who is asked does not just agree. The request is passed to the team leader, who checks it is safe and allowed, works out the extra cost and time, and agrees it with the client and the manager as a variation, in writing, before the work is done. The change is recorded on the drawings. This protects the client, the company and the team from misunderstandings, and keeps the job on budget.
markingPoints: One agreed contact speaks to the client
Regular updates on progress, problems and power shut-downs
Change requests passed to the leader, not agreed on the spot
Changes checked, priced and agreed in writing as a variation
Changes recorded on drawings; explains why this protects everyone

essays.stem: Describe the responsibilities of a Level 3 member in a self-managed electrical team.
essays.modelAnswer: A Level 3 member is responsible first for their own work: doing it safely, correctly and on time, to the drawings, the specification and good practice, and testing and recording it honestly. They follow and enforce safe isolation and other safety rules, and stop work that is unsafe. They help plan the team's work, set targets and share tasks fairly. They support less experienced members by coaching and checking their work, giving constructive feedback. They take part in solving problems, using facts rather than blame. They communicate clearly with the team, the client and other trades, and report progress, problems and changes to the manager in good time. They look after tools, test instruments and materials. They also keep learning and suggest improvements to the way the team works.
markingPoints: Own work done safely, correctly, tested and recorded honestly
Follows and enforces safety rules; stops unsafe work
Helps plan, set targets and share work
Coaches and checks less experienced members
Communicates and reports; looks after equipment; suggests improvements

essays.stem: Explain how you would coach a less experienced team member to terminate steel-wire armoured cable, while making sure the job's quality is not put at risk.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan the coaching at a time when the job allows it, and start on an off-cut rather than the real installation. I would explain the steps and why each matters, then show the full termination slowly: measuring and marking, removing the sheath, cutting the armour without nicking the bedding, fitting the gland and earth tag, and terminating the cores. Then the member does one while I watch and ask questions, and I give clear, positive feedback and point out what to improve. When their practice pieces are good, they move on to the real job, and I check each termination before the enclosure is closed, together with the tests. I would increase their independence step by step. I would record their progress on the skills matrix, so the team knows when they can work alone. This builds the team's skills while the inspections protect the quality.
markingPoints: Plans the coaching and starts on practice pieces
Explains and demonstrates the steps and the reasons
Watches the member practise and gives constructive feedback
Checks real terminations and tests before they are closed
Increases independence step by step and records progress on the skills matrix

essays.stem: Your team's monthly figures show that 12% of circuits failed their first test, two jobs finished three days late, and there was one near miss with a ladder. Explain how the team should review these results and plan improvements.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should meet to review the figures together, without blaming people, and look at each one in turn. For the 12% first-test failures, it looks at which tests failed and why, for example loose terminals or damaged insulation, using a simple tally to find the most common cause. It then agrees actions, such as a second-person check before testing, and a target to reduce failures. For the late jobs, it compares the plan with what happened and finds the causes, such as late materials or underestimated time, and agrees better planning or earlier ordering. For the near miss, it finds out what happened with the ladder, checks the ladder and the way it was used, and agrees controls such as footing the ladder or using a platform, and a toolbox talk. Each action has an owner and a date. Next month the team checks the figures again to see if the actions worked.
markingPoints: Reviews the figures as a team without blame
Finds causes of test failures and agrees actions and a target
Finds causes of late jobs and improves planning or ordering
Investigates the near miss and agrees safety controls
Gives each action an owner and date, and checks results next month

essays.stem: Explain how a self-managed electrical team should work with other trades and the site manager on a building site.
essays.modelAnswer: The team should find out the site rules and the overall programme from the site manager at the start, and go to the site coordination meetings. It plans its work to fit with the other trades: for example, conduits and boxes go into walls before the plasterers arrive, and cables are drawn in after the roof is on so they stay dry. It agrees routes with the plumbers and air-conditioning fitters early, using the drawings, so services do not clash. It keeps its work area tidy and safe, protects its finished work, and warns others before isolating supplies or doing anything that affects them. It respects other people's work and does not cut or move it without agreement. Problems, such as another trade damaging cables, are reported to the site manager with facts and photos, not argued over on site. Good relations save time and rework for everyone.
markingPoints: Learns site rules and programme; attends coordination meetings
Sequences work to fit with other trades
Agrees routes early to avoid clashes
Keeps area safe, protects work, warns others of isolations
Reports problems to the site manager with facts rather than arguing

essays.stem: Explain why self-managed teams can work better than closely supervised ones, what can go wrong in them, and how a team can stop those problems.
essays.modelAnswer: Self-managed teams can work better because the people doing the job make many of the decisions, so problems are solved quickly on the spot. Members feel more responsible for their work and take more pride in it. Skills spread because members share tasks and train each other, and the team can change its plans fast when something changes on site. However, things can go wrong. Without clear limits, a team may make decisions it should not, such as changing a design. Some members may do less while others carry them. Safety can slip if everyone thinks someone else is checking. Arguments can grow if there is no agreed way to settle them. The team can prevent these problems by agreeing ground rules and its limits of authority in writing, setting clear targets, rotating roles such as safety lead, checking each other's work, holding regular reviews, and reporting to the manager.
markingPoints: Gives benefits: faster decisions, ownership, shared skills, flexibility
Names risks: overstepping authority, uneven effort
Names risks: safety slipping, unresolved conflict
Prevention: ground rules, limits of authority and targets
Prevention: rotating roles, peer checks, reviews and reporting

practical1.title: Self-managed installation of lighting and socket circuits on training bays, with group lock-off and peer inspection
practical1.brief: As a self-managed team, plan and install a lighting circuit with two-way switching and a radial socket circuit on the training bays, from the drawing and job sheet given by the assessor. First, hold a short planning meeting: set a target time, share the tasks using a simple skills list, and name a planner, a safety lead, an inspector and installers, rotating roles halfway through so every member does at least two roles. Before any work on the bay's distribution board, isolate it as a group: the safety lead switches off, every member fits their own padlock and tag to a multi-lock hasp, and the safety lead proves dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after. Keep a progress board up to date. When the work is done, a member who did not install each circuit inspects it and initials the check sheet, and the team carries out continuity, insulation resistance and polarity dead tests and records them. Every member removes their own lock at the end. The instructor carries out any switch-on and function test. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training bay with a distribution board, isolator and multi-lock hasp
One padlock and danger tag per member
Conduit or trunking, cable, two-way switches, lamp holder or fitting, socket outlets and boxes as the drawing shows
Hand tools, crimp tool and torque screwdriver
Continuity and insulation resistance tester, and test record sheets
Drawing, job sheet, skills list, role rota and a progress board (whiteboard or flip chart)
photos: The planning meeting, with the role rota and target on the progress board
The isolator with every member's lock and tag on the hasp
Proving dead, with the tester on the proving unit
The circuits during installation, showing different members at work
The peer inspection check sheet with initials
The completed test record and the finished circuits
checklist: Took part in planning and setting the team's target
Fitted their own lock and tag, and removed only their own lock at the end
Did at least two roles as the rota set out
Installed their share of the work neatly and to the drawing
Inspected another member's work honestly and recorded the result
Took part in the dead tests and recorded results correctly
Kept the progress board up to date and communicated with the team
safety: Never work on the board until every member's lock is on and it has been proved dead with a tester checked before and after
Only the instructor energises the circuits, after the dead tests have passed
Use stepladders as the Centre's rules say, with a second person footing them
Keep the work area tidy and off-cuts in the bin

practical2.title: Team fault-finding on a dead training board, with a root-cause review and action plan
practical2.brief: The assessor has set four faults on a training board (for example an open circuit, a reversed polarity, a high-resistance joint and a low insulation reading) and gives the team a 'customer complaint' sheet. As a self-managed team, the group first agrees a plan and shares out the circuits. The board is isolated, locked off and tagged, and proved dead with a tester checked on a proving unit before and after; it stays dead for the whole task. Each member locates at least one fault using dead tests only (continuity, insulation resistance and polarity), records the readings, and photographs the fault once found. The team then holds a short review: it lists the faults on a tally sheet, asks why each might happen on a real job, and agrees one action to stop each one happening again, with an owner and a date. One member presents the findings to the assessor while the others answer questions. The assessor checks the repairs. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Training board with faults set by the assessor, a lockable isolator and a multi-lock hasp
Padlocks and danger tags, voltage tester and proving unit
Continuity and insulation resistance tester, or multifunction tester used on its dead tests only
Customer complaint sheet, fault log, tally sheet and action plan form from the assessor
photos: The team's plan, with circuits shared out
The isolated, locked and tagged board, and the tester on the proving unit
Each member taking a test reading
Each fault once found, before it is repaired
The completed fault log and tally sheet
The action plan and the presentation
checklist: Took part in planning the search and sharing the work
Followed the isolation procedure and kept the board dead
Used the right dead test to find their fault and recorded the reading
Repaired their fault neatly and retested it
Took part in the review, using facts rather than blame
Helped agree an action with an owner and a date

safety: The board stays isolated, locked and tagged for the whole task; prove dead with a tester checked before and after
